Everyday batteries & power markets

ESS tenders and battery trends

Understand LFP growth in global energy storage and Korea's ESS central contract market.

ESS stores electricity for later use

An Energy Storage System (ESS) includes batteries, a power conversion system (PCS), controls, cooling and fire protection. It smooths renewable output and shifts electricity supply to periods of higher demand. MW measures instantaneous power; MWh measures stored energy. A 100 MW / 600 MWh system provides roughly six hours of rated output under rated conditions.

In new battery storage installations worldwide, LFP lithium-ion batteries are currently the most common. The IEA reports about 80% of new storage in 2023 and over 90% of new stationary battery installations in 2025. These figures refer to new installations worldwide, not the share of all installed ESS capacity in Korea.

IEA · LFP share in 2023 ↗IEA · Stationary installations in 2025 ↗

Which batteries are gaining ground, and why?

TransitionWhy this choice?Continuing roles & challenges
Lead-acid → wider lithium-ion useLead-acid is inexpensive with established supply and recycling, but is heavy and has limitations in usable energy and cycle life. Lithium-ion offers advantages in efficiency and installation space.Lead-acid has not disappeared. It remains in UPS and backup-power applications.
NCM and NCA applicationsHigh energy per unit mass and volume, supported by mature Korean supply technology. Useful where installation space is limited.Thermal management, raw-material prices and operating conditions matter. Korean and global markets evolve at different speeds.
Growing LFP shareLFP contains no nickel or cobalt and offers long cycle life and relatively high thermal stability. Stationary ESS faces fewer weight constraints than vehicles, so lifetime cost often matters more than energy density.Lower energy density, cold-weather performance and state-of-charge estimation remain challenges. LFP can still catch fire, so system safety design is essential.
Exploring sodium-ion, flow batteries and moreMaterial options and long-duration storage needs drive interest. Flow batteries allow tank capacity and system power to be sized relatively independently.These technologies have not replaced the global ESS mainstream. Cost, efficiency, footprint and supply scale still need validation.

This does not mean every ESS has switched from NCM to LFP. LFP is increasingly selected for new investments. Samsung SDI presents NCA in SBB 1.7 and LFP in SBB 2.0; LG Energy Solution also offers NCM(A) and LFP. Compare lifetime electricity delivered, efficiency, replacement and operating costs alongside battery prices when selecting a system.

What is Korea's ESS central contract market?

Korea Power Exchange announces required locations and capacity. Developers bid a price and a plan to build and operate ESS. Selected projects provide storage and delivery capability under a contract and receive settlement payments. This is separate from battery product procurement and hydrogen-generation HPS/CHPS tenders.

  1. Tender announcementLocation, power and energy requirements
  2. Project proposalPrice, site, equipment and safety plan
  3. Evaluation & selectionPrice and non-price assessment
  4. Construction & verificationPermits, installation and performance checks
  5. Operation & settlementMeet contracted availability obligations

The September 22, 2026 notice seeks mainland capacity of 1,100MW·6,600MWh and Jeju capacity of 80MW·480MWh, each sized for six hours of storage. Target completion is February 2029. The mainland notice specifies a 15-year term with 50 points for price and 50 for non-price factors, including safety, technical performance, grid and industrial contributions. Tender capacity is not awarded capacity.

Choosing LFP does not automatically win a contract. Evaluation covers fire prevention and response, certification, efficiency, life and grid conditions, as well as chemistry. The notice does not permit mixing NCM and LFP within one bid configuration.

The tender price unit, KRW/kW-h, is a contract and settlement unit tied to available power and time. It must not be directly compared with battery purchase prices in KRW/kWh. This explanation is dated October 5, 2026; consult the original notice for current participation and submission requirements.
